item.title: Triangles and quadrilaterals suffice
item.description: arXiv:2610.13986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a conjecture proposed by Robert J. Lang over 20 years ago, stating that in a circle-packed origami design, any axial polygon with 5 or more sides can be reduced by properly adding a new circle. The proof is based on the structure of the medial axis of the region enclosed by the circles, and yields a concrete algorithm for finding the added circle. The result extends to configurations involving rivers.
item.dc:creator: Mu-Tsun Tsai

item.title: Philip L. Roe, the British Scientist. The Cranfield Years and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2610.14087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Philip L. Roe, the renowned British scientist, passed away on April 26, 2026, at the age of 87, while Professor Emeritus at the University of Michigan. My association with Phil Roe began in 1984, when he joined the Cranfield Institute of Technology, UK, as Professor of Computational Fluid Dynamics, while I was a postdoctoral research fellow at the same institution. For more than four decades, his incisive ideas, physical principles and distinctive approach to research on numerical methods for solving hyperbolic partial differential equations have had a lasting influence on my own approach to research in the field. Here I recount some personal memories and anecdotes emerging from the rewarding experience of interacting with Phil during the Cranfield years and beyond. I also review, quite succinctly in places, some of the main research topics that he pursued throughout much of his academic career. These notes are intended as a modest homage to Roe's impact on the subject, as well as to his influence on the careers of generations of scientists in both academia and industry.
item.dc:creator: Eleuterio F. Toro

item.title: The Dialectical Theorem: The future of universities, mathematics departments, and training of human mathematicians
item.description: arXiv:2610.14362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the future of mathematics as a profession in a world where artificial intelligence may surpass human mathematicians in essentially every technical task. Through an informal dialogue, we explore why human mathematical expertise might nevertheless remain valuable, what kinds of expertise universities should cultivate, and how graduate education might adapt. We also discuss the institutional and economic uncertainties that threaten the continued existence of a thriving mathematical profession, even if the value of human mathematical understanding endures.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Koberda, Alex Kontorovich

item.title: Sharing a unit, measuring a length: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for fractions from Grade 1 to Grade 8
item.description: arXiv:2610.14735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractions require learners to revise properties associated with whole numbers. This paper presents a design rationale and a critical analysis of an eight-level source progression for fractions (Grades 1-8, nominal ages 6-14), from which the French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. Its central hypothesis is a bridge from sharing to numerical measure: a share of one unit is represented by a bar, read as a length relative to a specified unit, and located on the number line. The reference unit is kept stable in the initial tasks to focus attention on fraction magnitude, equivalence and operations; changing the unit is deliberately postponed, without treating this as a mathematical requirement or an established reduction in cognitive load. Three principles organise the meanings: sharing one unit, coordinating bars and number lines, and establishing fractions as numbers before explicitly treating them as scalar operators. Two supporting principles concern valid local justifications before formal generalisation and chains of equalities, introduced in Grades 2-3, with written reasons in lessons from Grade 4. The analysis relates these choices to the research literature and selected curricula, examines task strategies and feedback, and distinguishes realised features from discrepancies and proposed revisions. The source documents and their curriculum projections do not establish the order actually experienced by pupils. No empirical evaluation is reported. Primary hypotheses address transfer between representations, coordination of units and the numerical status of fractions before operators; the audit also identifies limits to the reproducibility of its findings.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Tariel-Adam

item.title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
item.description: arXiv:2610.17090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset. We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey. We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.
item.dc:creator: Ying Xie

item.title: A Central Limit Theorem for High-Temperature SYK Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.18440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model is a quantum many-body model of Majorana fermions with all-to-all random interactions. It has attracted wide interest in condensed matter and high-energy physics as a solvable model of non-Fermi liquids and holography. Fix an even integer $q\geq4$, and let $Z_N(\beta)$ be the partition function of the Gaussian $q$-body SYK model. We prove that for all sufficiently small inverse temperatures $\beta > 0$, there exists $\rho=\rho(\beta)>0$ such that \[ N^{q/2 -1}(\log Z_N(\beta)-\mathbb{E}[\log Z_N(\beta)]) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\rho^2). \] In addition to the mathematical results, we discuss how the proofs were developed and refined through interaction between human researchers and AI, and we describe the subsequent formalization of the main arguments in Lean 4. This work thus serves as a case study of a research workflow that integrates human insight, AI-assisted exploration, iterative proof refinement, and formal verification.
item.dc:creator: Yoshinori Kamijima, Shuta Nakajima, Ryoichiro Noda, K\^{o}hei Sasaya

item.title: Probability and statistics in Greece
item.description: arXiv:2607.07147v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Official statistics in Greece started as early as 1828 with the first Census. A department of statistics was established in 1861, and the General Statistical Service of Greece was founded in 1925. It was reformed to become the National Statistical Service of Greece in 1953, which was then replaced by the independent Hellenic Statistical Authority in 2010. The science of probability and statistics was essentially introduced in the late 1960s and before 1982. Seven chairs, plus were established in probability and statistics, albeit with various names, at the four Greek universities and ASOEE, which existed then, and six aspirants were elected to the post of professor of the respective chair. Since 1982, when the law abolished the archaic system of chairs, more than 200 PhD holders in probability and statistics or related subjects have been elected or promoted to the new ranks of professor, associate professor, and assistant professor at the 25 public Greek universities, which exist today. Several of these professors or associate professors have been elected to the post of Rector or Vice Rector. Now, probability and statistics, as well as related subjects, are very well treated in Greece. Today, the Greek contribution to these specialties is internationally recognized
item.dc:creator: Andreas N. Philippou, Apostolos Kasapis, Alex Karagrigoriou
